content: Vitiligo is a chronic dermatological condition characterized by the loss of skin pigmentation in a patchy distribution. Some individuals report experiencing pruritus (itching) prior to the emergence of new depigmented patches. This condition can affect individuals of any age or ethnicity, with over half of the cases manifesting before the age of 20. Vitiligo is classified into two primary types: generalized vitiligo, which presents symmetrically across the body, and segmental vitiligo, which is confined to one side of the body. Globally, approximately 1% of the population is affected by vitiligo, which results in the appearance of white patches on the skin. While various treatment modalities exist, none are curative, though some can achieve repigmentation. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of all therapeutic interventions used in the management of vitiligo. The search for relevant studies was updated to October 2013 and included databases such as the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, AMED, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and LILACS. Additionally, five clinical trial registries were searched, and reference lists of included studies were reviewed for further randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The review included RCTs that assessed the effects of treatments for vitiligo. At least two independent reviewers evaluated the eligibility and methodological quality of the studies and extracted data. This update incorporated 96 studies, including 57 from the previous review and 39 new studies, with a total of 4,512 participants. Most studies had fewer than 50 participants and evaluated a wide range of interventions. All studies assessed repigmentation, but only five addressed all three primary outcomes: quality of life, achieving greater than 75% repigmentation, and adverse effects. Among secondary outcomes, six studies evaluated the cessation of disease progression, but none assessed the long-term durability of repigmentation at two years post-treatment. Combination therapies generally demonstrated superior outcomes compared to monotherapies. New interventions included seven surgical techniques. Data from 25 studies addressing primary outcomes were analyzed. Effect measures such as risk ratio (RR) and odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were used. Only one of nine studies assessing quality of life showed no statistically significant improvement between treatment groups. Nine analyses from eight studies reported greater than 75% repigmentation, with combination therapies often outperforming monotherapies. For example: Calcipotriol combined with PUVA (psoralen with UVA light) was more effective than PUVA alone (OR 4.25, 95% CI 1.43 to 12.64; one study, N = 27). Hydrocortisone-17-butyrate with excimer laser was superior to excimer laser alone (RR 2.57, 95% CI 1.20 to 5.50; one study, N = 84). Oral minipulse of prednisolone (OMP) with NB-UVB (narrowband UVB) was more effective than OMP alone (RR 7.41, 95% CI 1.03 to 53.26; one study, N = 47). Azathioprine with PUVA outperformed PUVA alone (RR 17.77, 95% CI 1.08 to 291.82; one study, N = 58). 8-Methoxypsoralen (8-MOP) with sunlight was more effective than psoralen alone (RR 2.50, 95% CI 1.06 to 5.91; one study, N = 168). Other findings included: Ginkgo biloba was more effective than placebo (RR 4.40, 95% CI 1.08 to 17.95; one study, N = 47). Clobetasol propionate was superior to PUVAsol (PUVA with sunlight) (RR 4.70, 95% CI 1.14 to 19.39; one study, N = 45). Split skin grafts with PUVAsol were more effective than minipunch grafts with PUVAsol (RR 1.89, 95% CI 1.25 to 2.85; one study, N = 64). A meta-analysis of three studies comparing NB-UVB to PUVA found a non-significant 60% increase in the proportion of participants achieving greater than 75% repigmentation in favor of NB-UVB (RR 1.60, 95% CI 0.74 to 3.45; I² = 0%). Topical treatments, particularly corticosteroids, were associated with the most adverse effects. However, in combination therapies, it was challenging to determine which specific treatment caused these effects. A pooled analysis of three studies comparing NB-UVB to PUVA found that NB-UVB was associated with fewer reports of nausea (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.69; I² = 0%; three studies, N = 156) and erythema (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.98; I² = 0%; two studies, N = 106), but not itching (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.60; I² = 0%; two studies, N = 106). Few studies focused exclusively on children or segmental vitiligo. One study evaluated psychological interventions, but its outcomes could not be included in the statistical analyses. No studies were identified that assessed micropigmentation, depigmentation, or cosmetic camouflage. In conclusion, while some evidence supports the efficacy of existing therapies for vitiligo, the findings are limited by variability in study designs, outcome measures, and the lack of quality-of-life assessments. Further high-quality RCTs using standardized measures are needed to evaluate the long-term permanence of repigmentation and to address the impact of treatments on quality of life.
